title: Does a longer base change the third angle?
description: Two angles of sixty degrees and seventy degrees are made at the ends of a base of five centimetres, and the third angle is read with the protractor. The same is done with a base of seven centimetres. Keeko's doubt is that a longer base gives a bigger third angle.
teaching_notes: One idea: once two angles of a triangle are fixed, the third angle is fixed too, whatever the length of the side between them. Watch for students who think a bigger triangle has a bigger angle.

source: Let us take two angles, say 60° and 70°, whose sum is less than 180°. Let the included side be 5 cm. What could the measure of the third angle be? Does this measure change if the base length is changed to some other value, say 7 cm? Construct and find out.
video_script.why: The child can draw a triangle from two angles and the side between them and now asks whether the third angle depends on the length of that side.
video_script.substitution: The book's own angles of sixty and seventy degrees, with a base of five centimetres and then seven centimetres.
video_script.anchor: a base with sixty degrees at one end and seventy degrees at the other, first five centimetres long and then seven centimetres long
video_script.wrong_answer: a longer base gives a bigger third angle
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees the longer base make a bigger triangle and expects its third angle to be bigger too, but the bigger triangle is a stretched copy with the same angles.
video_script.payoff_line: The third angle is fifty degrees for both bases

final_answer.spoken: the third angle is fifty degrees for both bases, so it does not depend on the length of the side

maths_rules: base 5 cm with 60° at A and 70° at B: the arms cross at C and the angle at C measures 50°
base 7 cm with 60° at A and 70° at B: the arms cross at C and the angle at C again measures 50°
the triangle with the longer base is a bigger copy of the first: every length is scaled but the angles are the same
